summary:
Santa Catarina stands under the national framework of Brazil. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change, and joint and second-parent adoption were confirmed by the Supreme Federal Tribunal in RE 846.102 (2015). A visitor's entry, documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as any other traveller's.

Discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds are punishable as equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989 following the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2019 ruling in ADO 26. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically in visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, and foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes.

Santa Catarina's own constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, yet as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Trans-specific protection in the state rests on the national constitutional and criminal provisions rather than on the wording of the state charter.

Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific law prescribes this. The Superior Court of Justice has ruled that non-binary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity, and gender-marker changes proceed without surgery.

Courts in the state have applied family protection to foreign partners. In Florianópolis, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian.

A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas of Santa Catarina may present more social friction, though legal rights are identical nationwide.

The wider national environment remains contested. A deeply conservative Congress has generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013, while constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions continue to apply nationwide and cover visitors in Santa Catarina.

On health care, the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee in September 2025, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy.
tangentialFactors:
Santa Catarina's constitutional text is narrower than the national regime it sits inside: the 2002 clause names sexual orientation but, as of 2019, not gender identity, whereas the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2019 ruling places transphobia on the same footing as racism. A trans visitor's protection therefore comes from federal provisions rather than from the state charter's wording.

Settled law coexists with legislative turbulence. Anti-LGBTIQ proposals in the national Congress, including attempts to repeal marriage equality, signal pressure on rules that are currently in force and applied to visitors.

Social climate varies within Santa Catarina. Florianópolis has pride events, active community organisations and legal professionals experienced in LGBTQ+ family and document matters, while smaller cities and rural parts of the state may carry more interpersonal friction despite identical statutory rights.

The reinstatement of the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee in September 2025 indicates that inclusive health policy again has an official channel for input, a protection that operates alongside the criminal-law guarantees.

Residents of Santa Catarina are protected at state level by a constitutional anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among its grounds. That clause did not extend to discrimination against transgender people as of 2019, leaving trans residents to rely on national constitutional and criminal provisions.

Since 2020, people in Santa Catarina have obtained identity documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices in the absence of any specific statute authorising it, a route reinforced by the Superior Court of Justice ruling that non-binary people may amend their civil registry. Name and gender-marker changes proceed without surgery.

Family law for residents follows national precedent: joint and second-parent adoption were confirmed by the Supreme Federal Tribunal in RE 846.102 (2015), and same-sex marriage has been available since 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013.

State courts have intervened in residence matters affecting same-sex couples, as when a Florianópolis judge barred the deportation of an Italian citizen partnered with a lesbian Brazilian after more than a decade together.

Residents also gained a formal voice in health policy when the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee was reinstated in September 2025, five years after its dissolution in 2019, to shape and monitor inclusive public-health measures.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory supplies Santa Catarina-specific figures on violence against trans people, hate-crime prosecutions, police complaints or court outcomes under ADO 26. Enforcement of the national provisions within the state is unresolved.

Whether Santa Catarina has enacted state-level penalties or a state hate-crime statute covering gender identity beyond Law 7.716/1989 is not sourced here.

The currency of the finding that the state constitution does not address discrimination against transgender people is unresolved beyond 2019; no later amendment or case law on the point is cited.

Visitors' practical access to gendered facilities, restrooms and identity screening at Santa Catarina airports or in state venues is not addressed by any source in the inventory.

It is not sourced whether the 2002 constitutional clause has ever been invoked in litigation on gender-identity grounds, or how state authorities handle complaints laid under it.
